utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Greetings to counsel and to everyone else in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution Douglas Stringer, Alexis Demirdjian, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, our intern Ms. Marija Bukovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to take care of that. It's okay now? Thank you. Mr. Stringer, I think there are a few procedural issues or matters you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian has those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian will take care of it. Okay. Sorry. Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. You may have seen some of the e-mail circulation in the last few days. Let me begin with one of the oral applications that I wished to make, and I've consulted with my learned friends from the Defence, and I believe they'll be able to state their position. First of all, in relation to a sketch or a layout of the Vukovar Hospital which we've proposed as a 65 ter 6405, we wish to use this image which was taken last year at the hospital, and it basically is a sketch of the hospital showing what it was like in 1991. I spoke to my learned friend Mr. Gosnell about the matter, and I believe he has no objections provided that we lay the foundations in advance and ask the witness to describe the hospital before displaying the image. So that's the first application I have, to add the document to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. No objection to using the document provided that -- and the issue is annotations. As long as any annotations that are on the document are first raised with the witness and the witness attests to the information in the annotations. Provided that's done, we wouldn't have any objection to the document being admitted after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we can -- we can add it to the exhibit list and then see what happens and whether it can be tendered or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do understand you correctly. So granted as prayed. The document can be added to the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. You may also recall that on the 28th of March we filed our eighth motion to amend the 65 ter list of exhibits. In that motion, there is a document that I wish to use with the next witness, and that is 65 ter 6402. These are minutes of a joint commission for tracing missing persons and mortal remains of the 2nd of April, 1992. There are similar minutes of the joint commission meetings on our 65 ter list. This is one of those that we obtained recently from Osijek I believe the county court. We obtained those documents at the end of March and we filed a motion on the 28th. I believe that the Defence has not had a moment yet to respond to this issue. I spoke to Mr. Gosnell about the matter. I think he wishes to take some time today to take a look at it, and in principle I believe there are no objections but I believe he wants the rest of the afternoon to take a look at this document. So that's one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this would mean that we would take a decision tomorrow after having heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Gosnell. Is that okay with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. To put the matter shortly, we reserve our position for the moment. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And -- great. There's also the issue of the faxes and letters that the next witness had sent throughout the time of the conflict, and essentially in relation to those, you may have seen an e-mail I sent out this weekend proposing that we display a number them and show them through the witness without having to go through each and every one of them. I believe there's around 40 -- roughly around 40 of them. I would like to use perhaps about 15 to 20 of them in court with the witness, and for the rest of them, considering that the content is pretty much similar in substance except that it's different dates, we wish to propose to tender them after having shown a certain number of them. And again, I will leave Mr. Gosnell to state his position, but I believe there's no objection to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct. There's no objection to that procedure. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Nothing to decide for the moment I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. And there's one last matter. During the course of the weekend as we were proofing Dr. Bosanac, she provide us a DVD, and this DVD contains handwritten -- there are scans of handwritten notebooks. These notebooks were compiled by one of the nurses at the Vukovar Hospital, and according to Dr. Bosanac they were taken by the Yugoslav People's Army when they took over the hospital on the 19th or 20th of November. These documents were not available to the Vukovar Hospital until last year. Apparently a meeting was held between the Serbian and Croatian government in the fall of 2011, during which these notebooks were hand over, and only a year later the Vukovar Hospital was able to obtain these notebooks. So the DVD contains scanned versions of these notebooks, and at this stage considering that we received it only a couple of days before the witness testifies, I do not wish to get into the substance. However, I would like to have your leave to show the documents on the screen to the witness for her to identify them, simply identify them, and later this week we will file a motion seeking leave to add these documents to the list, and we could also hear from the Defence at that stage, and perhaps we will tender them through a bar table motion. So I'm kind of doing the opposite of MFIing a document. I'm asking her to identify the material with are a view to adding it to the list and having them tendered at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We do object to this. This is in effect trying to MFI documents before they're even on the 65 ter list. We're dealing with document -- there have been a great number of documents over the years of this nature that have been disclosed. It's a great burden on the Defence to go through these documents and now we have yet another iteration. I don't know precisely why these documents would only have come to light late in last year. There's been no explanation, no information about that. So given the state of information at the moment, we object to -- we object to using it, first of all prior to it being on the 65 ter list, and in due course, we probably will object to it being put on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, why -- why would you like to show them to the witness before a decision has been taken to add them to the exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could ask questions to the witness in abstract, asking her, "Did you provide us a CD? Does this CD contain such-and-such material?" That could be done. I just thought that for purposes of identification it might be relevant for Your Honours to see the document and for her to identify this is what she provided us over the weekend. That is all I wish to do at this stage. But if you believe that identification is not necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to -- I'm just trying to understand your motion requesting the addition to the exhibit list would come in when? Would the witness be away?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- I can try to get this done before the witness leaves. I cannot promise this at this stage, but if it would help in this matter, I can make an effort to file the motion tomorrow afternoon perhaps. And I believe the witness will still be here until Wednesday at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, let's try to get this right and have the request to add it to the exhibit list before the witness is asked anything about the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that be all, Mr. Demirdjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We can call our next witness, Dr. Bosanac, GH-038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness can be brought in. While we are waiting for the witness, I would like to instruct the OTP -- can you -- can you wait just one moment, please. In the last few months the Trial Chamber has dealt with a variety of motions of the Prosecution for the admission of various items of documentary evidence. Too often the documents being tendered by the Prosecution are either not available on e-court or otherwise not ready for determination of the Trial Chamber. For example, missing translations. The Trial Chamber has had to expend an inordinate amount of time identifying these problems, bringing them to the attention of the Prosecution, and then monitoring the Prosecution response to the identified deficiencies. The Chamber recalls that it requested the Prosecution via e-mail in October last year to ensure that its standard documents are translated and made available on e-court. However, this situation still persists. It is not the responsibility of the Trial Chamber to remedy the deficiencies of the Prosecution in this area. The Trial Chamber again directs the Prosecution to ensure any document it is tendering as evidence is uploaded to e-court, translated, and in all respects ready for a determination on its admission. An e-mail communication will follow shortly regarding the latest situation wherein tendered documents are not ready for a determination of the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I don't have access to the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to solve that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, in the meanwhile can I proceed with the solemn declaration for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'll follow the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Madam Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your first name and family name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vesna Bosanac. I was born on the 9th of March, 1949. I am Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalty of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration the usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Bosanac. I see that the chair you're sitting on doesn't seem to be very comfortable. Could we have some assistance from the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The chair is too high for me. It has to be lower down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Bosanac, I will start with my questions, and if at any moment a question is not clear, please don't hesitate to ask me to repeat it, and as I told you, we'll be going until 7.00 today, so if you get tired or need any break you can tell us or you can address the Judges. First of all, could you tell us what is your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I am the CEO of the hospital in Vukovar, and I also treat children. This is my profession. I'm a paediatrician.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you give the Judges a brief description of your educational background.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I completed grammar school in Vukovar, and I graduated from the school of medicine in Zagreb. In 1981 I completed my residency in paediatric medicine, and then in 1983 I obtained my master's degree. From 1974, I worked in the medical centre in Vukovar, and in 1991, in the month of July, I was appointed the CEO of the medical centre. From 1991 to 1997, I worked in exile. I was affiliated with the health care ministry, and then after 1997, after the peaceful reintegration, I returned to Vukovar, and I currently work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Judges a little bit about the Vukovar Hospital. When was the hospital built, and when did it start functioning?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The Vukovar Hospital was built in 1849. That was the first time it was developed. At that time, it was a very small hospital. It occupied one part of the summer house of Count Eltz, and then it was extended in 1939. It was operated by the Sisters of Mercy from Djakovo. In its present form it was developed in 1974. During the war, it was significantly damaged, practically destroyed. It was refurbished in 2011. It was redeveloped, and it has assumed its present shape and form.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the Vukovar Hospital, is that also referred to as the Vukovar Medical Centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The Vukovar Medical Centre functioned up until 1993, and then the reform of the health care system started in Croatia whereby hospitals were separated from medical centres so that now the Vukovar Hospital is a hospital, whereas the outpatient clinics which provide primary care all belong to the Vukovar health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Judges how many buildings were located in the hospital's compound.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Within the compound there is a total of five buildings which accommodate patients. Two of them are main hospital buildings featuring beds and departments where the patients are treated. We call them the new hospital building and the old building. Moreover, there is a department for physical therapy, there is an outpatient clinic where the patients are examined, there is a pathology and cytology department, as well as the department which provides food for the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I like to display an aerial image of this area. It is 65 ter 6315, and that is at tab 109 of our list. Doctor, in a moment I will ask you to annotate certain parts of the image you'll see on the screen. First of all, do you recognise this area on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the hospital compound with the buildings and the environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. With the assistance of the usher, I will ask you to make some markings now. Now, could you mark on this with the letter A the new hospital building you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And with the letter B the old one.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we see some streets here. Are you able to situate them a little for us?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is one of the main streets. It's called Zupanijska street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you put the letter C for that one.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what is the street below Zupanijska street?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This one here is called Gunduliceva street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, you marked this with the letter D. Now between the old building and the new building, what is it that we see there? It looks like a parking lot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, it's a green surface, and there's a monument now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Are there any buildings in here which belong to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, as I said before, there's this department for physical therapy, and across the park there is the kitchen and the department of pathology and cytology. And behind that is an atomic shelter where we spent most of our time during war working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would you mind marking these with individual letters following the letter D. E, F, G, et cetera. Perhaps starting with the last one you mentioned, the area where the atomic shelter was. If you can mark that with the letter E.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: There is an axis path from that yard which goes from the old building to the new building. Subterranean passage, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And I believe that is sufficient for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6315 as marked by the witness will be Exhibit P1421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If I take you back to 1991, Dr. Bosanac, how many floors did the main building have at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: There was a basement, the ground floor, two floors, and a loft or attic which was not used by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to your office as of July 1991 as a director of the hospital, in which building was your office located?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: For a while the administration building was outside the hospital compound, across this street where the old hospital building is. However, very early on in August, that building was completely destroyed by the shelling, and then I moved my office to the underground floor of the main hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time in 1991, could you tell the Court how many rooms were there in the main building, and what was the maximum number of patients the hospital could have taken during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In the main building on those three floors that were in use, the ground floor and the first and the second floor, there were 250 beds, whereas in the old building we also had a high ground floor and two storeys where we could put up in peacetime an additional 150 patients. However, already back in August, the hospital was constantly targeted by the shelling and bombing, so that from 15 August on, we were able to work only in the basements. It was too dangerous even in the higher ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court during peacetime how many staff members were working at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: One thousand and forty employees, but at that time we were all part of the medical centre. There were the physicians, the nurses who worked in outpatient clinics, ambulances, et cetera. So in total there were 1.040 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that -- the shelling of mid-August. How did that shelling affect, if in any way, the number of staff members at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Even before that, in June and in July, many employees left the hospital. It was the normal vacation time, but it coincided with the beginning of the war. Already on the 2nd of May, wartime began in Vukovar. In June and July, shells were falling on Borovo Naselje and the Borovo factory, and many employees left their jobs. Generally speaking, there were many employees of all ethnicities in the hospital, Serbs, Croats, Ruthenians. Vukovar was a multi-ethnic town. Nineteen ethnicities were represented, but many, many left at that time. Many Serbs left, going across the Danube to Serbia. A large number of Croats left for other parts of Croatia where there was no war. So that in August only about 350 of us remained in the hospital, including the medical staff and auxiliary staff also of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You just mentioned that Vukovar had about what was 19 ethnic groups. Could you tell the Court which groups were represented -- well, had the highest representation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, the city of Vukovar had a population of 45.000, and the entire area around us, which is now the eastern part of the Vukovar-Srem county, it was then called Vukovar, it had 147.000 population. Forty-seven per cent were Croats, around 35 or so per cent were Serbs, and the rest were different ethnicities, Ruthenians, Ukrainians, Slovaks. There was also a group that declared themselves as Yugoslavs, and those were mainly people who were in mixed marriages or children of mixed marriages so that they declared themselves as Yugoslavs, and there were about 5 per cent of them in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, prior to the conflict, can you describe to the Trial Chamber what was the relationship between those various ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I worked as a paediatrician for many years there by that time, and I can say that as I saw it, there were no inter-ethnic conflicts, neither in the population at large or among the staff of the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did that situation change at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- if you would allow me just one little question. Ms. Bosanac, how do you define one's ethnicity? I mean, what makes someone to be a Croat and what makes someone to be a Serb or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our regulations, everyone determines their own ethnicity. It's a matter of choice, and it's usually linked to tradition. If your family, your father, mother, and other relatives are all Croats, then you declare yourself as a Croat. There are cases where the marriage was mixed between a Croat father and Serb mother. The children of such a marriage would declare themselves as Croat or Serb or Yugoslav. Other national minorities such as Ukrainians and Ruthenians also declared themselves as they chose according to their own tradition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's how people declare themselves. And how about other people defining someone? Would you -- would you go to someone and ask him whether he defines himself as a Croat or a Serb, or are there other criteria that allows someone to determine the ethnicity of someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I'll be able to give you a precise sense to this question, but I heard there was some regulations in the former Yugoslavia whereby in the registers of population of registers of voters, ethnicity would be entered according to where their fathers happen to be in a certain year. That's something I only heard about. But in every census you would get a blank, a form, where you would write down your name, surname, date and place of birth, your ethnicity, your confession. You can write all that, but you don't have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But that's still what you do yourself about your own ethnicity. I mean, how -- how do you determine the ethnicity of your neighbour, for instance? How do you know he is a Croat or a Serb, because he told you, because of his religion, because of something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that before the war and even now after the war people in Vukovar do not look at each other in terms of ethnicity. They don't judge each other by ethnicity. Some people feel the need to say to what ethnic group they belong, others don't. Throughout all my work, and now it's been 15 years that we returned to Vukovar, in our archives where we have records of employees we never write ethnicity. We just right down the name and surname, their educational attainment, address of residence, et cetera. We do not write down ethnicity or religion. That is, I suppose, written into the registers of birth after censuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one minute, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Witness, picking up on the Presiding Judge's question. Yes, Ms. Witness, after hearing the question of the President, when you -- [Overlapping interpretation] ethnicity. It's a bit difficult for me to understand what that means, that you have Croat nationality or that you are Croat even without the nationality of that state. When you are Croat, you can be, for instance, Serb by ethnicity or something else by ethnicity, or a national of another country. How is one supposed to know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where we live, ethnicity is one thing and nationality is another. Those are two different concepts. You can be Croat while being a national of Croatia or a national of Serbia or a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you are an ethnic Serb, you can also be a national of Croatia, of Serbia, or of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or some other country, Germany or the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, we left off where we were asking about the relationship between the ethnic communities, and my question to you was: Was there a time where this relationship changed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Certainly. As the war began, there occurred changes in the ethnic structure. Although in the town of Vukovar where there were 45.000 inhabitants before the war, during the encirclement in the aggression only 15.000 remained. In the encirclement, those people who remained in town and in the hospital included all ethnicities, but when Vukovar fell, when the Yugoslav Army entered Vukovar along with all sorts of paramilitaries who came with the army, they divided people thoroughly so that Serbs were free. They were free to go to Serbia or to remain in Vukovar, whereas most of the Croats and other non-Serbs ended up in camps. During the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina from 1991 through 1997, when the peaceful reintegration began, most of the population in Vukovar and around the environs, which was called the Croatian Danube valley, was part of the Osijek and Baranja counties, most of the population was Serbs, although there were some remaining Croats, Hungarians, and members of some other ethnic minorities. However, in that period of 16 years, the national minorities and people in mixed marriages were subjected to all sorts of torment and torture that I know about from witnesses and some I -- I witnessed. In 1997 when we returned, we found 25.000 residents -- in fact, that's the number that required medical assistance. That's how I know the number. And that's when returnees started to arrive. The past 15 years has been a time of restoration and return, and the area is again multi-ethnic. The structure is slightly altered, but again members of various ethnicities live in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to take that answer you gave us and go back a little bit in time. Was there a point before, because you talked about the conflict and the fall of Vukovar, et cetera, was there a time before the conflict start where there were indications of a change in the relationship between the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's true. Practically from 1988, changes began in the former Yugoslavia, changes that were supposed to lead to political transformation in terms of making individual republics independent. The former Yugoslavia was made up of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, Montenegro, and Serbia with its two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo. After Tito's death, all sorts of changes began. I remember that. I was a student at that time. Yugoslavia, as you know, was a socialist country with a ruling Communist Party. All sorts of liberal ideas started to sprout. Talk about liberalisation began. Croatia and Slovenia were foremost in this, and very soon negotiations began about the transformation of Yugoslavia. The presidents of Slovenia and Croatia wanted the country to be transformed into a confederation. However, the political forces in Serbia, which was headed by Mr. Milosevic, and some other republics were against that, and at that time centralisation was pervasive in Yugoslavia in every way, in payments, in the foreign currency system, and the changes began in the late 1980s and early 1990s that resulted in the independence of certain republics. As for Vukovar, we could also feel those changes. Vukovar was at that time a rather advanced city doing very well, very progressive. We had a factory that employed over 10.000 people. Around Vukovar and in the hospital and elsewhere, in Borovo, we had 15.000 people employed in a rather well developed industry, but the socialist system was showing its weaknesses. Money was running short. Many industries were unable to deal with the new free market economy. Pay was late. Salaries were not paid, and there were all sorts of changes that had nothing to do with ethnicity. However, the Milosevic regime, at least this is how I see it, took advantage of that moment to advance the idea of Serbian hegemony and started spreading it through rallies beginning with Kosovo and Knin and parts of Croatia. They were spreading constantly some ideas among the Serbian people that they are threatened. They were spreading some myths that they are in danger, that all of Yugoslavia has to be one great Serbia, and that's when national rifts, divisions along ethnic lines began. In our area as well. The settlements around Vukovar had a majority Serb population, and Serb volunteers rushed in as if to purportedly protect them. Roadblocks were put up under that pretext, and the Yugoslav Army was arming those volunteers and the Serb population who thought that under the leadership of Slobodan Milosevic they would succeed in occupying the greatest part of Yugoslavia so as to make it one big Serbia. That's how the war began in the former Yugoslavia, and we were very hard hit by all that in Vukovar. All the more so because we did not expect the heavy devastation that eventually happened. We were hoping for a political solution and that the crisis would be resolved peacefully. However, from August until November, hundreds of thousands of bombs and projectiles and shells handed on the town. A lot of the city was damaged. Many people were killed, so that very early on we felt in our own skins the aggression that is difficult to imagine if you were not in Vukovar at that time. Later on, the war spread to other parts of Croatia, and in 1992 to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but those early days in Vukovar, the very start, was really the heaviest, the fiercest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to take you to a specific -- sorry. I'd like to take you to a very specific event. It is an agreed fact between the parties that there is an incident on the 2nd of May, 1991, in Borovo Selo. Are you familiar with this incident?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, although at the time I was not the CEO of the medical centre, but I do remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How did you come to learn about it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That I was on duty in the outpatients' clinic in the hospital. My nurses spoke to some other nurses on the phone. They lived in Borovo Selo. They said that they couldn't come to work because there was shooting going on. The situation was very dramatic. Everybody was afraid. In the afternoon they started bringing wounded and dead. They were all police officers from Borovo Selo. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And following this, could you explain to the Judges what was the security situation like during the month of May and June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: At that time, in the month of May, after that incident, the situation in Vukovar was still calm. There was no shelling. However, the roadblocks had already been put up. You could not take your customary roads to go to Osijek or elsewhere. You had to pass through the barricades or you had to use some roundabout ways. That caused us a lot of problems with the transport of patients. I remember that. And people from the villages who had to come to the hospital because they worked there had to have passes. For a while they kept on coming to work but then they stopped. In the month of June the situation became more difficult. The first shells started falling on the Borovo factory and Borovo village, especially in the month of July. And in August, the shells started falling on the city of Vukovar itself on the central part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that in the month of July you were appointed as the director of the medical centre in Vukovar. Could you tell us who was the director before you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The director of the Vukovar Medical Centre before me was an elderly doctor. His name was Rade Popovic. At that time, he resigned. I remember that very well. I was a member of the workers council. That was the name of the management board of the medical centre. When he resigned, he handed in his notice, and he said that he didn't want to continue serving as a director. Later on I learned that the minister had asked for his resignation because he tolerated the fact that many people had stopped coming to work, especially from Borovo Selo. When I took over his position, I realised that that was indeed true and that many people had stopped coming to work from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You learned that the minister had asked him to resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on that note I would like us to display 65 ter 206, which is at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the subject here says "Request to Dismiss the Director, Dr. Rade Popovic." Could you tell the Court who sends this document and who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: As you can see from the heading, it was the healthcare ministry which sent this letter in July 1991 to the president of the workers council of the medical centre. At that time, the president of the workers council was Dr. Vojislav Stanimirovic. He was the one who called the workers council meeting. I was a member of that body. But at that time I was not aware of this document. I only saw it later. And at that meeting, Dr. Popovic told us that he was handing in his resignation because he no longer wanted to occupy that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if we scroll down to the bottom of page 1 in both versions, does this document explain the reasons behind the request of the Ministry of Health?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I learnt this letter only subsequently, and I realised that Dr. Popovic was being asked to resign because he turned a blind eye to the fact that many people did not come to work, and they did not have a justification, and he didn't dismiss them. At that time in July, people were on legitimate leaves, but they were supposed to return, which they did not. I suppose that somebody advised the minister of that, and the minister then asked for Dr. Popovic's resignation, and Dr. Popovic resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we turn page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise the signature on this letter?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is Professor Hebrang's signature. He was the health minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Following his resignation, could you tell the Court what happened to Dr. Popovic, the former director?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: He remained working as the head of a department. I was then appointed the acting director of the hospital. The workers council actually elected me based on a proposal. There were three candidates running. I gained the majority of the votes. I was then appointed the acting director of the medical centre, and then Minister Hebrang, complying with the rules, confirmed my appointment as the director of the medical centre. Dr. Popovic told me that he would help me, that he would remain working, that I could rely on him and his experience, and he remained working despite the hardships and the war activities. Later on he went to Montenegro, and he could not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make an application to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 00206 will be Exhibit P1422. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor -- sorry. Thank you. Doctor, you explained the situation was increasingly tense during the months of June and July. I'd like to take you to the month of August and describe what was the situation in the town of Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Shells started falling on the city centre in August. I remember that during the first week of August two shells fell near the market where a doctor of ours resided. His house was there. He came to tell us that and he said that he was packing to go to Germany. Many people left Vukovar at the time. In the hospital we established our own Crisis Staff. My assistant were Dr. Ivankovic, the head of surgical department; Dr. Kuzmanovic, the head of the outpatients' clinics; Mr. Krstic who was the assistant director for finances. We held our meetings every two or three days. We organised the supply of medicines and medical equipment. I would go to Zagreb to talk to Professor Hebrang. I would talk to him about the situation and how much medical equipment and supplies were need because our storages were completely empty. I learned later on that some nurses had taken all those from the hospital and that they later on set up their own outpatients' clinics in Serbian villages. In any case, we tried to gather as much assistance as we could. We organised ourselves so that everybody worked all the time. A decree came from the main medical staff to the effect that nobody could leave their posts, and if they did and if they did not report to work for five days, they would be dismissed from work. That was a war decree that was signed by the head of that medical staff, Ivo Prodan, and that was cosigned by Minister Hebrang. That's how we organised ourselves. We drafted an evacuation plan so that all the patients who were at the hospital at the time could be lowered down into the basement within 15 minutes. And all the chronical patients who did not require constant medical care were evacuated from Vukovar. For example, the patients who were on dialysis for -- because of the renal failure were sent to Rovinj in Istria. All patients had to be sent to various hospital departments we did, and those that we could treat were treated in our hospital. We set some rules that we all complied with, and we managed to organise work even in the direst of circumstances. From the 15th of August we could not leave the basement at all because there was daily shelling and shells kept on falling on the hospital day in and day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, you mentioned the shelling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, it is that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are we going until quarter to or? We started at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Quarter to? Okay. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So, Doctor, you're talking about shelling. Can you tell the Court if you know who was doing the shelling?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: At that time, Vukovar was already encircled and shells were launched from the left bank the Danube from the eastern and southern parts of the city. There were air-strikes, and all those were bombs and shells launched by the JNA, or, actually, they all belonged to the JNA, but I don't know exactly who launched those shells and bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, are you familiar with events at the post office in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I remember that. We learned that the post office had been hit, that people were wounded there. Military transporters were roaming the city all the time. They then arrived at that hospital. I don't know why. I remember an event when a military APC arrived in the hospital to fetch a newborn baby and the parents had been left behind a roadblock. I don't know where they were, either in Bobanja [phoen] or Trpeta [phoen]. The baby was small. We tried to explain to them that the baby should be kept in hospital until it reached a certain weight. However, one day an APC arrived and a military doctor was with them. They came to fetch the baby to my great astonishment. They could have used a normal car, but, no, they did not. They used an APC. Then we realised that we were in a war zone and that things could only get worse from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video-clip which is 65 ter 4798.6. That's at tab 90 of our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And for our interpreters, you may have a bundle. It's at tab A of your bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The army caused another incident in the Vukovar post office on August the 20th. Three civilians were killed in the gunfire and the investigation by the joint commission established that apart from the Yugo-soldiers, nobody else shot a bullet. That day the Croatian children started to return from their summer holidays."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, on this image do you recognise any of the medical staff by any chance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is our ambulance which was sent to the spot in August. We already had 20 people who had been brought in for war injuries. Some of them were civilians and the others were Croatian policemen who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The first returnees are already exposed to the terrorist attacks of the Vukovar's fifth-columnists."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you were mentioning earlier that military vehicles were in the streets. What do you see here on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I can see an APC of that -- of the kind that used to roam the streets of Vukovar. One of them arrived at the hospital as I already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. We can play the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] On the --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. You can shut it down. Thank you. Your Honours, may I make an application to tender this video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4798.6 will be P1423.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the midst of all this, Dr. Bosanac, you were explaining to us that people were leaving the town. Can you tell us specifically if anything specific was done with the children in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Of course I remember. As I say, it was the time of summer holidays. Children were on holidays at the seaside. I remember that Serbian children left Serbian villages. I couldn't believe my eyes when I saw them leaving. I didn't know why they were leaving. I remember a nurse who was from Negoslavci who used to work with us. She was on night-shift. Her husband called her to tell her to come home immediately because buses had arrived from Sid to take the women and children to Sid. She had just come to work. She couldn't believe what she heard. He -- she told him not to send her children anywhere before she came. The following day she went home and she never returned. I suppose she was taken to Sid. I remember some of my patients from Borovo Selo who phoned in to arrange a check-up and they could not come for their check-ups because they wouldn't allow them. They forced them to go to Vojvodina. And I remember those children who were returned from their holidays hoping that they would start school on the 1st of September or in any case at the beginning of September. I remember that Mr. Vlatko Pavletic was the minister of education. He held a press conference. He said that the situation would calm down, that the negotiations were underway, and that school would start. The situation was very confusing. A lot of children returned to Vukovar, whereas many children left, predominantly of Serbian ethnicity. Children of both ethnicities stayed in Vukovar. I remember because I lived there. And we kept on expecting that the situation would calm down. Of the 15.000 people who remained in Vukovar, there were about 1.500 children under the age of 15. Later on that was a big problem. When shells started falling, we had to protect those children. We had to keep them under lock in atomic shelters and basements in order to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you mentioned earlier the issue of the shelling of the hospital. Did the hospital take any measures to indicate or demonstrate that this building was indeed a hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I've already testified about that on a number of occasions. On the roof of one of its buildings which housed the infectious disease department there was a huge red cross, and the green area between the new and the old hospital buildings we also spread a large piece of white cloth depicting a red cross. Later on it turned out it was a good target, because shells kept on falling close to that red cross. And then people kept telling me why don't you remove that red cross? Maybe they would not go on shelling us that much if the cross wasn't there. No rules were observed during that war. It was aggression by the so-called JNA and all the paramilitaries that accompanied it. It was just inconceivable what happened to us, what we suffered at their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to show you a video now which is at 65 ter 4970.1. This is at tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And for the interpreters, you will find the transcript under tab C.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you rewind it just a little bit. Right there. We'll get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, what do you see on this image?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I can see one of those APCs belonging to the JNA. It arrived within the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what's the building in the background?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is the May hospital -- the main hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, this is 7 seconds into this clip. We can keep playing it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] This is how the Yugoslav Army treats the facilities which are so clearly marked with a red cross."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That's the sheet that we spread. One of them was on the roof and the other one was on the ground between the old and the new hospital buildings. It was spread on the green surface between those two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how large was it, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it was large. Perhaps 7 metres by 9 metres. It covered the entire green surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you freeze here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you able to see the date on this clip, Doctor? Maybe we can play it a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Not really, no. I know it's 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I can see it. 28 August, 1991, or perhaps 26th August, 1991, at 9.54.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, we heard the shelling on this clip. Is this representative of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Fully. It lasted the whole day from morning 'til night. I counted the shells and bombs. There were over a hundred that fell into the hospital compound every day. Thousands of them fell in the city. Vukovar is on the right bank of the Danube and it spreads over 10 kilometres, and it was completely encircled and shells kept on falling on us all day. Only from time to time we had a calm night. I would go to work every morning at 6.00, and no sooner did I arrive a new casualty started arriving, and then around noon I would go home when it was calm, and incendiary flares could be seen during the night from across the Danube or from Negoslavci. In any case, the whole sky was ablaze. It was like a fireworks display.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would make an application to tender this video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 4970.1 will be Exhibit P1424.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I notice the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Bosanac, we'll take the first break now. We will come back at 15 -- sorry, at 16.45 -- yes, of course, 16.15. Thank you. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, your motion for that video that the witness provided you with, could you file that by, let's say, 1.00 tomorrow, and then we would ask the Defence to give a response by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're working on it, and I believe we are in a position to do it by 1.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that be okay with you as well, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Welcome back, Doctor. You explained to us before the break that you had placed a red cross flag on the hospital compound and that some of your colleagues suggested to remove it because it was becoming the target of shelling. I would like to show you a short clip which is 65 ter 4970.2. This is at tab 26. There is no transcript for this one. It's a very short two-second clip. We can play it now, just pause right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with this image?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened within the hospital compound. The bomb fell just next to the canvas with the red cross on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours, would I ask to tender this document -- this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4970.2 will be Exhibit P1425. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, earlier you explained that the shelling was coming from across the Danube and from the area of Borovo. Could you tell us whether the shelling was also coming from other parts of town?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said already, shells were coming in from the left bank of the Danube where tanks or cannons were entrenched. You could see them from our side of the river. They also came from the south, from the direction of Negoslavci, and after they encircled us, they came from Bogdanovci and Marinci, even stronger where the Yugoslav Army had cut off the roads. So we were being shelled from all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just to avoid a little confusion, in your question you asked the witness: "Could you tell us whether the shelling was also coming from other parts of town?" Do you mean other directions or other parts of town? What town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: From other directions into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Into the town, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on that you mentioned to us the left bank of the Danube. I would like you to take a look at an image which is 65 ter 6316 at tab 110. Thank you. Doctor, could you -- are you, first of all, familiar with this image, what we're seeing on the image?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. On this image which is an aerial photograph you can see the city of Vukovar. This part here is the River Danube flowing this way, which makes Vukovar on the right bank of the Danube. On the left bank where the cannons and the tanks that were targeting us. This here is the flow of the Vuka river which flows into the Danube. Here you can see the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps with the help of the usher you could mark everything you've indicated to us. First of all, could you put an arrow to show the flow of the River Danube. Maybe in the middle of the river itself just put an arrow.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when you meant the left bank of the Danube where you saw the tanks, where would that be? You could put the letter A in that area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you saw the hospital compound, could you put a letter B around that area.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You also mentioned there a river, Vuka, I believe. If you could put the letter C in that area.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you mentioned earlier that on the left bank where the cannons and the tanks were targeting us, this is where you indicated the letter A; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may make an application to tender this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked photograph will be Exhibit P1426.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Judges about the frequency of the shelling from mid-August onwards.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: On a daily basis, ever more and more, it was especially intensive in October and November. Every day over a hundred different projectiles fell on the hospital, shells, tank shells, and projectiles from multiple-rocket launchers, as well as air bombs. Every day. There was not a single day without shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us about the multiple-rocket launchers. How do you know that these were used at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I know because I saw it. I felt it. I went out from the hospital when 16, 20 projectiles were fired from one and the same weapon within a very short time. It was a horrendous thing. You could not not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, could you explain to the Judges how this shelling of the hospital impacted your work and that of the staff members at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The conditions were very hard indeed, because we were forced to operate only in the basement, underground. We put up sandbags against windows and boarded them up to be able to work, but under very difficult circumstances. When those armoured projectiles and air bombs fell, they would drill through the ground and disperse fragments. People ran away trying to find shelter in the deepest parts of the basement. There was no water. We had to collect water from wells around. We had several generators, and we brought some fuel oil to have power from -- for basic medical procedures such as X-ray, lab equipment, light for the operating room. The conditions were very hard, especially water shortages, and there were ever more and more wounded people. In the early days we were able to evacuate those more seriously injured to Vinkovci up to the end of September. However, in October and November we were completely besieged, so we could not evacuate anyone any more. We put up the less seriously injured in shelters in Borovo Komerc and other business premises to be able to accommodate serious patients. Gangrene cases were evermore frequent, and there were evermore problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like you to take a look at this next clip which is 65 ter 4970.3. This is at tab 97. There's no need for sound and there's to transcript for this. We'll just be looking at the image. And -- right. Yes, we can start playing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we pause here for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you able to see the date on this video?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, 5th October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And so far what have we seen? Do you recognise the compound?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: As we could see, this is the entrance into the hospital. This is the road between the new hospital building and the department of physical therapy which used to house the emergency room before. These are ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we pause here for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which building were we looking at just now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is the main building of the hospital, the surgical department. This is the time and the date when two air bombs fell on the hospital simultaneously. One of them exploded here on the second floor in the surgical ward. There were no patients there because the patients were all in the basement, but the damage was considerable. The entire building was shaking and trembling. Whereas, the second bomb penetrated all the five storeys from the roof down to the subterranean passage leading to the atomic shelter, and it fell exactly on a bed where a patient was lying. However, it didn't explode, so apart from terror and shock and the damage to all the floors above, it did not cause any casualties, only material damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, this is the 22nd -- no, 25 seconds mark on the clip. Let's keep playing it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we pause right here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the sandbags and the logs that protected the entrance to the underground floor, because the shells were falling from all directions all the time. So we were constantly trying to better protect this basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you can see a doctor operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like you to look at another clip -- well, just before I do that, Your Honours, can I tender this video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before it's admitted, could we ask the Prosecution whether they have any confirmation of the date counter on these videos? It may not matter at all, but if they do have any information that would assist on whether or not that's accurate --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, would you happen to know who recorded this footage?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This was filmed by one of our employees who had a video camera. He still works at the hospital. It's sure that this was filmed on the dates indicated. The time and date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any indications that the time is incorrect, or date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4970.3 will be Exhibit P1427. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look at the next clip which is 65 ter 4970.4, at tab 97. And this one we don't need the sound. There is no transcript either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we pause here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with what we are looking at at this stage?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: We see the inside of the hospital and the patients, the ill and wounded people, underground where everything was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, this is the 4 second mark. Let's keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this representative of the conditions that were prevalent at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. It was overcrowded. Here where you see a large number of patients, it's the corridor of the underground floor where patients were placed because in a way it was the safest place. What you see here are the empty rooms on the upper storeys, the first floor and the second floor. Nobody was there. We had moved everyone down back in August, in the basement. Here is the view from the upper floor of the area where the air bomb exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. May I make an application to tender that clip, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4970.4 will be Exhibit P1428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that an aeroplane bomb fell on the hospital, and it broke through several grounds, I believe. Could you look at this next clip, which is 4798.8, at tab 90.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you see the hole in the roof where the bomb fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And here what do we see?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is the hole created by the bomb that fell through the roof and on through all the floors until the subterranean passage leading to the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We can stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you explained earlier that the bomb pierced through but did not explode. But it fell, you told us, on the bed of a patient; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. In that subterranean passage beds had been placed, lined up, and the bomb fell onto the feet of the patient, crushing the bed, and he was practically glued to the bomb, and everybody was terrorised because they thought it was -- would explode. So I called the police, somebody from the bomb squad to inspect it, and they did and realised that the fuse was defective and it wouldn't explode. First of all, they detached the patient from the bomb, put him on a stretcher, and took him outside, and luckily the patient suffered only shock but no serious injury. After the fall of Vukovar, that man stayed in Vukovar and later on when we returned in 1997, he looked me up. I saw him again, and I wrote him a certificate about that incident, because he needed it for his own purposes as a civilian victim of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe there's a question from the Trial Chamber, but may I just clarify with the witness if she remembers the name of the patient and his ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember it, but I would not like to tell his name in public considering that I'm not a protected witness. If you want his name, according to the law on the rights of patients, then I would like to be given the opportunity to do so in private to respect his rights as a patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, may we go in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I believe Judge Mindua had a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a question. [Interpretation] My question is to you, Mr. Prosecutor, because I have the impression that there was a slight misunderstanding. On transcript page 36, lines 3 through 6, the witness spoke about air bombs. On page 38, she speaks of two air bombs that fell on the hospital. But you, Prosecutor, on page 40, speak of aeroplane bombs. I think it's different, because air bomb is a projectile that cannot be guided and hits randomly, whereas aeroplane bombs are dropped from planes during combat and can be guided. So what are we talking about, guided missiles or bombs that fell randomly on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be better to ask the witness herself to give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, could you explain to the Trial Chamber again the types of bombs that were targeting the hospital -- or sorry, that were hitting the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In this case those were air bombs. Those were bombs were launched from aeroplanes. I know what they looked like. They were big. It weighed over 250 kilos. It was almost the size of a patient -- a patient's bed. And that's, at least, what the experts from the police told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in addition to aeroplane bombs, you also described earlier different types of bombs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: As I've told you, on a daily basis all sorts of projectiles fell on the hospital, all sorts of bombs, and they incapacitated us almost incompletely. There was an armoured projectile that was launched from an aeroplane, and when it hit the ground, it exploded only then. So it completely filled in our subterranean corridor with concrete and soil. Almost a tonne of the material fell on a patient who was in a bed. We dug him out. We thought that he would be dead, but he survived. He was buried under the debris that weighed over a tonne. That patient had been -- was tetraplegic from before the war. He was brought to the hospital because he could not be looked after at home, and he almost got killed by that bomb, but he did survive and then after the fall of Vukovar, he was transported to Zagreb, and they gave him accommodation in a home. I know his name as well, but again I would not mention it in open session. I don't want to violate anybody's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I believe that the witness answered that they were air bombs which were launched from aeroplanes. Does this clarify the matter sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now it's absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this video-clip which was 4798.8?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4798.8 will be Exhibit P1429. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, earlier, Doctor, you told us that you were not using the upper floors of the hospitals as of the month of August or September, I believe. Could you tell the Court which parts exactly of the hospital you were using.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: We could use only the basement where we had organised our Emergency admission, the OR. First we had one and then two. Those were all both makeshift operating theatres. All of the basement rooms were redesigned and used as hospital rooms so that our patients lie on the floors in all of our basement rooms. There were some smaller rooms which were used to accommodate the staff during night. It was only rarely that the personnel could rest. Everybody was on duty all the time. All of the basement rooms in the main hospital room and in the old hospital building were occupied by patients. The same was true of the basement -- basement of the infectious diseases department which was in Vilaknolj [phoen] where patients were in all the basement rooms. We also had a makeshift kitchenette in the basement as well as a laboratory. The laundry room was there as well. The most important area was our atomic shelter, because that's where we could guarantee our patients almost a hundred per cent safety, and when shelling was the hardest, patients were safe in the atomic shelter. That's where our most serious cases were accommodated. It was an intensive-care unit. We also had a room for pregnant women and newborns, little babies in incubators. We had a room for wounded children. Currently those rooms house a museum, and if at all possible I would like to invite you to come visit that area to see what it looks like now and also there is a reflection on what it looked like at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you told us also earlier that your office moved from one building to the main building, I believe. On which floor was your office as of the month of September?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Again, in the basement. The basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I would like to use the sketch of the hospital which was added to the 65 ter list this morning. It is at tab 118 and it's 65 ter 6405. And there is an English version as well. However, for the purposes of the witness, I'm wondering if it would be more useful to zoom on the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with this image?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us exactly what we are looking at here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: We are looking at the floor plan of the basement, of the main hospital building. This was drafted by our matron. She organised a lecture. Actually, there was a lecture organised by the organisation of war nurses, and she was one of the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And approximately can you tell us when this sketch was prepared?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: She did it sometime in 1993, when we were already in Zagreb. That's where she was preparing her lecture. I don't know when exactly that was. It was in 1993. Here you can see the entrance into the emergency room. There was an outpatients' clinic where we did the triage of the wounded. There were two such rooms. This is the first OR. You could see a doctor operating here behind those wooden trunks. And this is a room for our Crisis Staff, and here behind that room there is a big window, and on the right-hand side where you can see beds this is the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, just a second. I think it would assist us if the usher could help you mark it, and perhaps if we zoomed out a little bit. Yes. The usher will assist you in marking this image. And if you could start again. You were first of all explaining to us --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is the entrance into the emergency room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
